promptTemplate: The bill is ${{billAmount}}. Using the double-the-10% trick, what is the 20% tip?
explanationTemplate: Move the decimal left: 10% of ${{billAmount}}. Double that for 20%. Two steps, done.

scenarioTemplate: You're at a restaurant. Your bill comes to ${{billAmount}}.
promptTemplate: What is {{tipPercent}}% of ${{billAmount}}?
explanationTemplate: Find 10% first — move the decimal left. Then build up: 10% + 5% + 3% = 18%, or 10% + 10% = 20%.

scenarioTemplate: You're settling the check after lunch with a friend.
promptTemplate: The check is ${{billAmount}}. What's the total after a {{tipPercent}}% tip?
explanationTemplate: Total = bill + tip. Tip = {{tipPercent}}% of ${{billAmount}}. Add both together.

scenarioTemplate: Your group of {{numPeople}} just finished dinner and agreed to split the bill equally.
promptTemplate: A ${{billAmount}} bill is split evenly among {{numPeople}} people. Each person's share of the {{tipPercent}}% tip is?
explanationTemplate: Calculate the full tip first: {{tipPercent}}% of ${{billAmount}}. Then divide by {{numPeople}} people.

promptTemplate: An item costs ${{itemPrice}} each. Buy 2 get 1 free. What's the per-item cost when you take the deal?
explanationTemplate: You pay 2 × ${{itemPrice}} for 3 items. Per item: (2 × ${{itemPrice}}) ÷ 3. The deal is 33% off, not 50%.

promptTemplate: An item costs ${{itemPrice}}. You use a buy-2-get-1-free deal to get 3 of them. How much do you save in total?
explanationTemplate: You pay for 2 and get 1 free — your saving is exactly 1 item's price: ${{itemPrice}}.

promptTemplate: A ${{originalPrice}} item gets {{firstDiscount}}% off, then your coupon takes an extra {{secondDiscount}}% off the sale price. Final price?
explanationTemplate: Apply discounts one at a time: ${{originalPrice}} − {{firstDiscount}}% first, then − {{secondDiscount}}% off that result. They don't simply add up.
scenarioTemplate: A store has a sale, and you also have a member coupon.

promptTemplate: A ${{originalPrice}} item has a {{firstDiscount}}% discount, then {{secondDiscount}}% off the discounted price. How much do you save in total?
explanationTemplate: Total saving = original − final price. The stacked saving is always less than {{firstDiscount}}+{{secondDiscount}}% — the second cut applies to the lower price.

scenarioTemplate: You set yourself a ${{budget}} discretionary budget for the month.
promptTemplate: Your budget is ${{budget}}. You've already spent ${{spent}}. How much do you have left?
explanationTemplate: Remaining = ${{budget}} − ${{spent}}. Simple subtraction — but tracking this in real-time is the whole skill.

promptTemplate: You have ${{budget}}. You buy {{quantity}} items at ${{itemPrice}} each. How much is left?
explanationTemplate: Spend = {{quantity}} × ${{itemPrice}}. Remaining = ${{budget}} − that total. Find the spend first, then subtract.

promptTemplate: A subscription costs ${{monthlyPrice}} per month. What does it cost over a full year?
explanationTemplate: ${{monthlyPrice}}/month × 12 months. Most people underestimate yearly costs because the monthly number looks small.

promptTemplate: An annual plan costs ${{yearlyPrice}} per year. What is the equivalent monthly cost?
explanationTemplate: ${{yearlyPrice}} ÷ 12. Compare this to the monthly plan price to see which is actually cheaper.

scenarioTemplate: You're deciding whether a purchase is worth it based on how often you'll actually use it.
promptTemplate: You spend ${{itemPrice}} on an item you plan to use {{numberOfUses}} times. What is the cost per use?
explanationTemplate: Cost per use = ${{itemPrice}} ÷ {{numberOfUses}}. A high price spread over many uses can be cheaper than a low price used rarely.

promptTemplate: A gym membership costs ${{itemPrice}} for the year. You realistically go {{numberOfUses}} times. What's your cost per session?
explanationTemplate: ${{itemPrice}} ÷ {{numberOfUses}} sessions. If this is more than a drop-in class costs, the membership isn't worth it.

promptTemplate: A ${{originalPrice}} item has {{taxPercent}}% sales tax. How much is the tax?
explanationTemplate: Tax = price × rate. Start with 10% of ${{originalPrice}} (move the decimal), then adjust down slightly for {{taxPercent}}%.

promptTemplate: You buy a ${{originalPrice}} item. With {{taxPercent}}% sales tax, what's the total?
explanationTemplate: Total = price + tax. Find {{taxPercent}}% of ${{originalPrice}} first, then add it to the original price.

promptTemplate: You grab {{quantity}} items at ${{itemPrice}} each. What's the total?
explanationTemplate: Total = price × quantity. ${{itemPrice}} × {{quantity}}: break it into rounds — double the price, then add extras.

promptTemplate: A pack of {{quantity}} items costs ${{totalPrice}}. What's the price per item?
explanationTemplate: Price per item = total ÷ quantity. ${{totalPrice}} ÷ {{quantity}}: divide evenly to find the per-unit cost.

scenarioTemplate: You're starting a new job and reviewing your offer letter.
promptTemplate: Your gross monthly pay is ${{grossPay}}. After {{deductionPercent}}% in deductions, what's your net (take-home) pay?
explanationTemplate: Net pay = gross × (1 − deduction%). ${{grossPay}} × (1 − {{deductionPercent}}%) = your take-home amount.

promptTemplate: A job offers ${{annualSalary}}/year. What's the approximate monthly gross pay?
explanationTemplate: Monthly pay = annual ÷ 12. ${{annualSalary}} ÷ 12 = monthly gross.

scenarioTemplate: Your manager just told you you're getting a raise. Now you want to know the real dollar impact.
promptTemplate: You earn ${{annualSalary}}/year and get a {{raisePercent}}% raise. How much extra money is that per year?
explanationTemplate: Annual raise = salary × raise%. ${{annualSalary}} × {{raisePercent}}% = extra per year.

promptTemplate: Your salary is ${{annualSalary}}/year. After a {{raisePercent}}% raise, what's your new annual salary?
explanationTemplate: New salary = old × (1 + raise%). ${{annualSalary}} × (1 + {{raisePercent}}%) = new annual pay.

scenarioTemplate: Your boss asks if you can work extra hours this week. You want to know what that's worth.
promptTemplate: Your regular pay is ${{regularRate}}/hr. You work {{overtimeHours}} hours of overtime this week. How much is your overtime pay?
explanationTemplate: Overtime pay = regular rate × 1.5 × overtime hours. ${{regularRate}} × 1.5 = ${{regularRate}} overtime rate, then × {{overtimeHours}} hours.

promptTemplate: Job A pays ${{weeklyPay}} weekly. Job B pays ${{biweeklyPay}} biweekly. How much more per year does the higher-paying job earn?
explanationTemplate: Job A annual = ${{weeklyPay}} × 52. Job B annual = ${{biweeklyPay}} × 26. The difference is the gap. Weekly has 52 pay periods, biweekly has 26.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{weeklySalary}} per week. What's your annual income?
explanationTemplate: Weekly × 52 = annual. ${{weeklySalary}} × 52 weeks = annual income.

scenarioTemplate: You deposit ${{principal}} into a savings account that earns {{interestRate}}% simple interest per year.
promptTemplate: You invest ${{principal}} at {{interestRate}}% simple interest per year for {{years}} years. How much interest do you earn in total?
explanationTemplate: Interest = Principal × Rate × Time. ${{principal}} × {{interestRate}}% × {{years}} years.

promptTemplate: You deposit ${{principal}} at {{interestRate}}% simple interest for {{years}} years. What's your total balance?
explanationTemplate: Total = Principal × (1 + Rate × Time). Add the interest earned to your original ${{principal}}.

scenarioTemplate: You're comparing savings accounts or investment options and wondering how long it takes for money to double.
promptTemplate: Using the Rule of 72, how many years does it take for money to double at {{interestRate}}% per year?
explanationTemplate: Rule of 72: years to double = 72 ÷ rate. 72 ÷ {{interestRate}} = {{answer}} years.

promptTemplate: You invested ${{cost}} and made a profit of ${{gain}}. What's your return on investment (ROI)?
explanationTemplate: ROI% = (gain ÷ cost) × 100. ${{gain}} ÷ ${{cost}} × 100 = your ROI.

promptTemplate: You invest ${{cost}} and earn a {{roiPercent}}% return. How much money do you make in profit?
explanationTemplate: Dollar return = cost × ROI% ÷ 100. ${{cost}} × {{roiPercent}}% = profit.

scenarioTemplate: Your bar tab for the night is ${{billAmount}}.
promptTemplate: You tip {{tipPercent}}%. What is the tip?
explanationTemplate: Tip = ${{billAmount}} × {{tipPercent}}%. Standard for bars is 18–20%. Always tip on the full tab, not just per drink.

promptTemplate: Your bill is ${{billAmount}}. You tip 10%. How much is the tip?
explanationTemplate: 10% = move the decimal one place left. ${{billAmount}} → 10% = just shift the decimal. This is the foundation of all tip math.

promptTemplate: Your bill is ${{billAmount}}. You want to leave a 15% tip. How much?
explanationTemplate: 15% = 10% + 5%. Find 10% (move decimal), halve it for 5%, then add. ${{billAmount}}: 10% + 5% = 15% tip.

promptTemplate: Lunch costs ${{billAmount}}. With a 15% tip, what is the total?
explanationTemplate: Total = bill × 1.15. Find 15% (10% + 5%) of ${{billAmount}}, then add to the bill.

promptTemplate: Your spa service costs ${{billAmount}}. You leave a 25% tip. What is the total bill?
explanationTemplate: Total = bill × 1.25. That's bill + 25%. 25% = bill ÷ 4. Add to original: ${{billAmount}} + (${{billAmount}} ÷ 4).

scenarioTemplate: A table of {{numPeople}} splits a ${{billAmount}} dinner bill equally, including a {{tipPercent}}% tip.
promptTemplate: How much does each person pay?
explanationTemplate: Each person pays (bill + tip) ÷ people. ${{billAmount}} × {{tipPercent}}% tip = total, then ÷ {{numPeople}} people.

scenarioTemplate: A group of {{numPeople}} goes out. The bill is ${{billAmount}} and they add a {{tipPercent}}% tip.
promptTemplate: What is each person's share of the total?
explanationTemplate: Per person = bill × (1 + tip%) ÷ people. Add {{tipPercent}}% to ${{billAmount}}, then split {{numPeople}} ways.

scenarioTemplate: You and a friend eat at a restaurant. The bill is ${{billAmount}}.
promptTemplate: You want to leave an 18% tip. How much is it?
explanationTemplate: 18% = 10% + 5% + 3%. Or: double the tax line (most states have ~9% tax). ${{billAmount}}: 10% + 8% = 18%.

scenarioTemplate: Your pre-tax meal is ${{billAmount}}. Sales tax is {{taxPercent}}%.
promptTemplate: You tip {{tipPercent}}% on the post-tax total. What is the tip amount?
explanationTemplate: Post-tax total = ${{billAmount}} × (1 + {{taxPercent}}%). Tip = that total × {{tipPercent}}%. Tipping on post-tax is slightly more than on pre-tax.

promptTemplate: A ${{originalPrice}} item has a 25% discount. How much is the discount?
explanationTemplate: 25% = ÷4. Halve ${{originalPrice}}, then halve again. That's your discount.

promptTemplate: A {{quantity}}-pack of yogurt costs ${{totalPrice}}. What is the price per cup?
explanationTemplate: Unit price = total ÷ quantity. ${{totalPrice}} ÷ {{quantity}} = price per cup. Knowing unit price lets you compare sizes fairly.

scenarioTemplate: A store runs a buy-2-get-1-free deal. Each item is ${{itemPrice}}.
promptTemplate: What is the effective cost per item when you take 3?
explanationTemplate: BOGO-3: you pay for 2, get 3. Effective price = (2 × ${{itemPrice}}) ÷ 3. That's a 33% discount per item.

scenarioTemplate: Store A sells an item for ${{originalPrice}}. Store B has the same item at {{discountPercent}}% off.
promptTemplate: What is Store B's price?
explanationTemplate: Sale price = ${{originalPrice}} × (1 − {{discountPercent}}%). That's what Store B charges.

scenarioTemplate: You have a ${{originalPrice}} item in your cart. You apply a {{discountPercent}}% coupon.
promptTemplate: After the discount, what do you pay?
explanationTemplate: You pay ${{originalPrice}} × (1 − {{discountPercent}}%). Non-round discount percents require careful math — break into 10% + remainder.

scenarioTemplate: A ${{originalPrice}} item is marked {{firstDiscount}}% off. At checkout, your member code gives an extra {{secondDiscount}}% off the sale price.
promptTemplate: What is the final price?
explanationTemplate: Stacked discounts multiply, not add. Final = ${{originalPrice}} × (1−{{firstDiscount}}%) × (1−{{secondDiscount}}%). Not the same as {{firstDiscount}}+{{secondDiscount}}% off.

promptTemplate: Your coffee order is ${{originalPrice}}. Sales tax is {{taxPercent}}%. How much is the tax?
explanationTemplate: Tax = price × {{taxPercent}}%. ${{originalPrice}} × {{taxPercent}}% = tax. For 10%: move decimal. For 8–9%: find 10%, adjust slightly.

scenarioTemplate: You're buying a ${{originalPrice}} gadget. Sales tax in your state is {{taxPercent}}%.
promptTemplate: How much sales tax will you pay?
explanationTemplate: Tax = ${{originalPrice}} × {{taxPercent}}%. Always calculate tax before you reach the register — especially on big purchases.

promptTemplate: A book costs ${{originalPrice}} before tax. Tax is {{taxPercent}}%. What is the total with tax?
explanationTemplate: Total = price × 1.{{taxPercent}}. Add {{taxPercent}}% to ${{originalPrice}}. At 10%, just add 10% (move decimal, then add).

scenarioTemplate: You're buying a ${{originalPrice}} item. The cashier will add {{taxPercent}}% sales tax.
promptTemplate: What total will appear on the receipt?
explanationTemplate: Total = ${{originalPrice}} × (1 + {{taxPercent}}%). Find {{taxPercent}}% of the price and add it. Always budget for tax on top of the sticker price.

promptTemplate: Two grocery items cost ${{priceA}} and ${{priceB}}. Rounding to the nearest $10, what is the estimated total?
explanationTemplate: Round each to the nearest $10, then add. Quick mental check before you reach the register.

scenarioTemplate: You grab two items off the shelf: ${{priceA}} and ${{priceB}}.
promptTemplate: Rounding each to the nearest $10, what is your estimated total?
explanationTemplate: Round each to nearest $10, then add. Fast estimation prevents register surprise on bigger purchases.

scenarioTemplate: You have ${{budget}} saved for gear. You buy {{quantity}} items at ${{itemPrice}} each.
promptTemplate: How much budget do you have left?
explanationTemplate: Remaining = budget − (qty × price). ${{budget}} − ({{quantity}} × ${{itemPrice}}) = what's left.

promptTemplate: A streaming service charges ${{monthlyPrice}}/month or ${{annualPrice}}/year. How much do you save per year by choosing the annual plan?
explanationTemplate: Monthly plan per year = ${{monthlyPrice}} × 12. Annual plan = ${{annualPrice}}. Saving = monthly annual cost − annual price. Always compare before auto-renewing monthly.

promptTemplate: You pay ${{monthlyPrice}} per month for a subscription. What is the total annual cost?
explanationTemplate: Annual = monthly × 12. ${{monthlyPrice}} × 12 = total yearly cost. Subscription costs add up — always know your annual spend.

scenarioTemplate: Your gym membership costs ${{itemPrice}} per year. You go {{numberOfUses}} times.
promptTemplate: What is your cost per visit?
explanationTemplate: Cost per visit = ${{itemPrice}} ÷ {{numberOfUses}} visits. Knowing this makes gym membership decisions obvious.

promptTemplate: You budget ${{budget}} for groceries. After spending ${{spent}}, how much is left?
explanationTemplate: Remaining = ${{budget}} − ${{spent}}. Simple subtraction — but knowing your budget number upfront keeps you on track.

promptTemplate: You pay ${{monthlyPrice}} a month for streaming. What does that cost you in a year?
explanationTemplate: ${{monthlyPrice}} × 12 = yearly cost. The monthly price is designed to feel small — always convert to annual to see the real commitment.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{monthlyIncome}} per month. What is your annual salary?
explanationTemplate: Annual = monthly × 12. ${{monthlyIncome}} × 12 = gross annual salary. Useful when comparing job offers quoted in monthly vs annual terms.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{hourlyRate}} per hour working full time (2,000 hours/year). What is your approximate annual salary?
explanationTemplate: Annual ≈ hourly × 2,000. ${{hourlyRate}} × 2,000 = approximate yearly salary. The 2,000 comes from 40 hours × 50 weeks.

promptTemplate: A salaried job pays ${{annualSalary}} per year. Assuming 2,000 working hours, what is the effective hourly rate?
explanationTemplate: Hourly ≈ annual ÷ 2,000. ${{annualSalary}} ÷ 2,000 = hourly equivalent. Use this to compare salary offers with contract or hourly jobs.

promptTemplate: Your biweekly gross paycheck is ${{grossPay}}. After a {{deductionPercent}}% deduction, what is your net pay?
explanationTemplate: Net = gross × (1 − deduction%). ${{grossPay}} × (1 − {{deductionPercent}}%) = take-home pay. Deductions include taxes and benefits.

scenarioTemplate: Your gross monthly salary is ${{grossPay}}. Taxes and benefits take {{deductionPercent}}% off the top.
promptTemplate: How much do you actually take home each month?
explanationTemplate: Net = ${{grossPay}} × (1 − {{deductionPercent}}%). Your take-home is always less than gross — plan your budget from net, not gross.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{annualSalary}} per year. You get a {{raisePercent}}% raise. How much more per year is that?
explanationTemplate: Raise amount = salary × raise%. ${{annualSalary}} × {{raisePercent}}% = additional annual pay.

promptTemplate: Your current salary is ${{annualSalary}}. You negotiate a {{raisePercent}}% raise. What is your new annual salary?
explanationTemplate: New salary = current × (1 + raise%). ${{annualSalary}} × (1 + {{raisePercent}}%) = your new salary.

scenarioTemplate: You currently make ${{annualSalary}} a year and just got a performance review.
promptTemplate: Your manager approves a {{raisePercent}}% raise. What is your new salary?
explanationTemplate: New salary = ${{annualSalary}} × (1 + {{raisePercent}}%). Knowing this in advance helps you negotiate confidently.

promptTemplate: Your regular pay is ${{regularRate}}/hour. You work {{overtimeHours}} hours of overtime at 1.5× rate. How much do you earn in overtime?
explanationTemplate: Overtime = regular rate × 1.5 × hours. ${{regularRate}} × 1.5 × {{overtimeHours}} = overtime earnings.

scenarioTemplate: You earn ${{regularRate}}/hour. This week you worked {{overtimeHours}} hours past your regular 40.
promptTemplate: How much will you earn for those overtime hours?
explanationTemplate: Overtime pay = hourly × 1.5 × OT hours. ${{regularRate}} × 1.5 = overtime rate, then × {{overtimeHours}} hours.

promptTemplate: You receive ${{biweeklySalary}} every two weeks. What is your annual gross salary?
explanationTemplate: Annual = biweekly × 26 pay periods. ${{biweeklySalary}} × 26 = gross annual salary.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{weeklySalary}} per week. What is your annual gross income?
explanationTemplate: Annual = weekly × 52. ${{weeklySalary}} × 52 = yearly total.

scenarioTemplate: A gig job pays ${{weeklySalary}} per week on average.
promptTemplate: If you work all 52 weeks, what is the annual income?
explanationTemplate: Annual = weekly × 52. ${{weeklySalary}} × 52. Useful when comparing gig income to a salaried offer.

promptTemplate: Your credit card balance is ${{balance}} with a {{apr}}% APR. What is your monthly interest charge?
explanationTemplate: Monthly interest = balance × APR ÷ 12. ${{balance}} × {{apr}}% ÷ 12 = your monthly charge. High APR makes even small balances expensive.

scenarioTemplate: You carry a ${{balance}} balance on your card (APR: {{apr}}%) and don't pay it off this month.
promptTemplate: How much interest will you be charged?
explanationTemplate: Monthly interest = balance × APR ÷ 12. At {{apr}}% APR, ${{balance}} costs you that amount in interest for just one month of carrying a balance.

promptTemplate: You carry a ${{balance}} credit card balance all year at {{apr}}% APR. How much interest do you pay annually?
explanationTemplate: Annual interest = balance × APR%. ${{balance}} × {{apr}}% = annual interest. This is why paying off your card monthly saves a lot.

scenarioTemplate: After a big purchase, your card balance sits at ${{balance}} all year (APR: {{apr}}%).
promptTemplate: What is the total interest cost for the full year?
explanationTemplate: Annual interest = balance × APR%. ${{balance}} × {{apr}}% = the total you pay in interest over 12 months. Carrying a large balance is very costly.

promptTemplate: Your credit card balance is ${{balance}}. The minimum payment is 2% of the balance. What is the minimum payment?
explanationTemplate: Minimum payment = balance × 2%. ${{balance}} × 2% = minimum due. This keeps you in debt longest — always pay more when you can.

scenarioTemplate: Your statement shows a ${{balance}} balance. The card requires a 2% minimum payment.
promptTemplate: What is the minimum amount due?
explanationTemplate: Minimum = balance × 2%. On ${{balance}}, that's a small amount — but at high APR, nearly all of it goes to interest, not principal.

promptTemplate: You take a loan with a ${{monthlyPayment}} monthly payment for {{numMonths}} months. What is the total amount you repay?
explanationTemplate: Total repayment = monthly payment × months. ${{monthlyPayment}} × {{numMonths}} = total paid. The difference from your original loan is pure interest.

scenarioTemplate: You borrow ${{loanAmount}} and repay ${{monthlyPayment}}/month for {{numMonths}} months.
promptTemplate: What is the total amount you repay over the life of the loan?
explanationTemplate: Total repaid = ${{monthlyPayment}} × {{numMonths}} months. Always compare this total to your original loan to see how much interest you're paying.

scenarioTemplate: You borrow ${{loanAmount}} and repay ${{monthlyPayment}}/month for {{numMonths}} months.
promptTemplate: How much interest do you pay in total?
explanationTemplate: Total interest = (payment × months) − loan amount. (${{monthlyPayment}} × {{numMonths}}) − ${{loanAmount}} = the bank's earnings on your loan.

promptTemplate: Your monthly income is ${{monthlyIncome}} and your total monthly debt payments are ${{totalDebt}}. What is your debt-to-income ratio?
explanationTemplate: DTI = (monthly debt ÷ monthly income) × 100. ${{totalDebt}} ÷ ${{monthlyIncome}} × 100 = your DTI%. Under 36% is healthy.

scenarioTemplate: You earn ${{monthlyIncome}}/month. Your rent is ${{totalDebt}}/month and you have no other debt.
promptTemplate: What is your housing debt-to-income ratio?
explanationTemplate: DTI = (debt ÷ income) × 100. ${{totalDebt}} ÷ ${{monthlyIncome}} × 100 = your housing DTI. Lenders prefer housing DTI under 28%.

scenarioTemplate: Your monthly income is ${{monthlyIncome}}. Your combined monthly debt payments (rent + loan) total ${{totalDebt}}.
promptTemplate: What is your debt-to-income ratio?
explanationTemplate: DTI = total monthly debt ÷ monthly income × 100. ${{totalDebt}} ÷ ${{monthlyIncome}} × 100. Lenders add all your debts together — not just one.

scenarioTemplate: Your gross monthly income is ${{monthlyIncome}}. You want to qualify for a mortgage with a ${{totalDebt}} monthly payment.
promptTemplate: What would your front-end DTI ratio be?
explanationTemplate: Front-end DTI = mortgage payment ÷ gross income × 100. Lenders want this under 28%. ${{totalDebt}} ÷ ${{monthlyIncome}} × 100 = your ratio.

promptTemplate: You pay an extra ${{extraPayment}}/month on a credit card with {{apr}}% APR. What is your approximate annual interest saving?
explanationTemplate: Annual saving ≈ extra payment × APR%. ${{extraPayment}} × {{apr}}% = approximate interest saved per year. This grows as your balance shrinks.

promptTemplate: Your balance is ${{balance}} at {{apr}}% APR. You make no payment this month. What is your new balance after interest?
explanationTemplate: New balance = old balance × (1 + APR/12%). ${{balance}} × (1 + {{apr}}%/12) shows exactly how carrying a balance grows your debt.

promptTemplate: You put ${{principal}} in a savings account earning {{interestRate}}% annual interest. How much interest do you earn in {{years}} year(s)?
explanationTemplate: Interest = principal × rate% × years. ${{principal}} × {{interestRate}}% × {{years}} = interest earned.

scenarioTemplate: You lend ${{principal}} to a friend at {{interestRate}}% simple interest per year.
promptTemplate: How much interest do you earn after {{years}} years?
explanationTemplate: Simple interest = principal × rate% × years. ${{principal}} × {{interestRate}}% × {{years}}.

promptTemplate: You invest ${{principal}} at {{interestRate}}% simple interest for {{years}} year(s). What is the total balance?
explanationTemplate: Total = principal × (1 + rate% × years). ${{principal}} + interest = new balance.

scenarioTemplate: You park ${{principal}} in a CD earning {{interestRate}}% simple interest.
promptTemplate: What is the account balance after {{years}} years?
explanationTemplate: Balance = principal × (1 + rate% × years). ${{principal}} grows by {{interestRate}}% each year.

promptTemplate: Your investment grows at {{interestRate}}% per year. Using the Rule of 72, how many years to double your money?
explanationTemplate: Rule of 72: years to double = 72 ÷ rate. 72 ÷ {{interestRate}} = {{answer}} years. Simple and surprisingly accurate.

scenarioTemplate: Your 401(k) has historically returned about {{interestRate}}% per year.
promptTemplate: Using the Rule of 72, roughly how many years will it take your balance to double?
explanationTemplate: 72 ÷ {{interestRate}}% = doubling time. At {{interestRate}}%, your money doubles roughly every 72 ÷ {{interestRate}} years.

promptTemplate: You invest ${{cost}} and sell for a ${{gain}} profit. What is your ROI percentage?
explanationTemplate: ROI% = (gain ÷ cost) × 100. ${{gain}} profit on a ${{cost}} investment = ROI of that %.

scenarioTemplate: You bought stock for ${{cost}} and sold it for a ${{gain}} gain.
promptTemplate: What was your return on investment (ROI)?
explanationTemplate: ROI% = profit ÷ cost × 100. ${{gain}} ÷ ${{cost}} × 100 = your percentage return.

scenarioTemplate: Your investment portfolio starts the year at ${{cost}}.
promptTemplate: After a {{roiPercent}}% gain, how much did the portfolio increase in value?
explanationTemplate: Gain = portfolio × return%. ${{cost}} × {{roiPercent}}% = dollar increase. This is the compounding base for next year.

scenarioTemplate: You invest ${{principal}} and leave it for {{years}} years at {{interestRate}}% simple interest.
promptTemplate: What is the total value of your investment?
explanationTemplate: Total = ${{principal}} × (1 + {{interestRate}}% × {{years}}). Patience is the most powerful investing tool.

scenarioTemplate: You buy a ${{itemPrice}} book and plan to re-read it {{numberOfUses}} times.
promptTemplate: You buy a ${{itemPrice}} book and read it {{numberOfUses}} times. What is the cost per read?
explanationTemplate: Cost per use = ${{itemPrice}} ÷ {{numberOfUses}} reads. Books are often very cheap per read when you re-use them.

scenarioTemplate: You buy a ${{itemPrice}} reusable water bottle and use it {{numberOfUses}} times before replacing it.
promptTemplate: What is the cost per use?
explanationTemplate: Cost per use = ${{itemPrice}} ÷ {{numberOfUses}} uses. Durable everyday items have very low per-use costs when you actually use them.

promptTemplate: You pick up {{quantity}} items at ${{itemPrice}} each. What is the total?
explanationTemplate: Total = price × quantity. ${{itemPrice}} × {{quantity}}: round the price to the nearest $1, multiply, then adjust.

scenarioTemplate: You want to understand what your credit card APR actually costs each month.
promptTemplate: Your balance is ${{balance}} and the APR is {{apr}}%. What is the monthly interest charge?
explanationTemplate: Monthly interest = balance × APR ÷ 12. ${{balance}} × {{apr}}% ÷ 12 = monthly charge. Even a small balance costs real money every month.

promptTemplate: Your credit card balance is ${{balance}}. The minimum payment is 2% of the balance. What do you owe as a minimum?
explanationTemplate: Minimum = balance × 2%. ${{balance}} × 2% = minimum due. Always pay more — minimum payments are designed to keep you in debt longer.

scenarioTemplate: You carry a balance and make no payment this month.
promptTemplate: Your balance is ${{balance}} at {{apr}}% APR. After one month with no payment, what is your new balance?
explanationTemplate: New balance = old × (1 + APR/12). ${{balance}} × (1 + {{apr}}%/12). Interest adds directly to what you owe each month you don't pay.

scenarioTemplate: You're reviewing your monthly credit card statement.
promptTemplate: Your balance is ${{balance}} (APR: {{apr}}%). How much is the interest charge this month?
explanationTemplate: Monthly interest = balance × APR ÷ 12. ${{balance}} × {{apr}}% ÷ 12 = the interest line on your statement.

promptTemplate: You take out a loan with a ${{monthlyPayment}} monthly payment for {{numMonths}} months. What is the total amount repaid?
explanationTemplate: Total repaid = monthly × months. ${{monthlyPayment}} × {{numMonths}} = everything you pay. Subtract the loan amount to find total interest.

scenarioTemplate: You borrow ${{loanAmount}} and pay it back in monthly installments.
promptTemplate: You borrow ${{loanAmount}}, pay ${{monthlyPayment}}/month for {{numMonths}} months. How much interest do you pay total?
explanationTemplate: Interest = total paid − loan. (${{monthlyPayment}} × {{numMonths}}) − ${{loanAmount}} = the lender's earnings. Always calculate before signing.

scenarioTemplate: You're applying for a new credit card and the lender reviews your finances.
promptTemplate: Monthly income: ${{monthlyIncome}}. Total monthly debt payments: ${{totalDebt}}. What is your DTI ratio?
explanationTemplate: DTI = debt ÷ income × 100. ${{totalDebt}} ÷ ${{monthlyIncome}} × 100 = DTI%. Lenders look for this under 36% for healthy borrowing.

promptTemplate: You pay an extra ${{extraPayment}} per month on a card with {{apr}}% APR. What is your approximate annual interest saving?
explanationTemplate: Annual saving ≈ extra × APR%. ${{extraPayment}} × {{apr}}% = interest avoided per year. Small extra payments have a big compounding impact.

scenarioTemplate: You leave a balance on your card all year and only pay the minimum.
promptTemplate: You carry a ${{balance}} balance for a full year at {{apr}}% APR. How much total interest do you pay?
explanationTemplate: Annual interest = balance × APR%. ${{balance}} × {{apr}}% = yearly cost of the balance. Paying it off saves this every year going forward.

promptTemplate: Your balance is ${{balance}} at {{apr}}% APR. You make no payment this month. What is the balance after interest?
explanationTemplate: New balance = ${{balance}} × (1 + {{apr}}%/12). One missed payment quietly grows your debt by that interest amount.

promptTemplate: Your monthly salary is ${{monthlySalary}}. Using the 28% rule, what's the maximum rent you should pay?
explanationTemplate: Max rent = ${{monthlySalary}} × 28% = ${{answer}}. The 28% rule keeps housing affordable.

scenarioTemplate: You just got a job paying ${{monthlySalary}}/month. You're apartment hunting.
promptTemplate: Using the 28% rule, what's the most you should spend on rent?
explanationTemplate: 28% of ${{monthlySalary}} = ${{answer}}. Quick check: a quarter of your salary plus a little.

scenarioTemplate: A friend says they spend 28% of their ${{monthlySalary}} monthly income on rent.
promptTemplate: How much rent do they pay each month?
explanationTemplate: 28% of ${{monthlySalary}} = ${{answer}}. That's a healthy housing-to-income ratio.

scenarioTemplate: You're comparing apartments. Your take-home pay is ${{monthlySalary}}/month.
promptTemplate: What's the maximum monthly rent you can afford under the 28% guideline?
explanationTemplate: Max rent = ${{monthlySalary}} × 28% = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: You're budgeting for the year ahead. Monthly salary: ${{monthlySalary}}.
promptTemplate: Using the 28% rule, what's the most you should spend on rent for the full year?
explanationTemplate: Monthly max = ${{monthlySalary}} × 28%. Annual = that × 12 = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Your rent is ${{currentRent}}/month. Your landlord raises it {{increasePercent}}%. How much is the monthly increase?
explanationTemplate: Increase = ${{currentRent}} × {{increasePercent}}% = ${{answer}} more per month.

promptTemplate: Rent goes from ${{currentRent}} up by {{increasePercent}}%. What's the new monthly rent?
explanationTemplate: New rent = ${{currentRent}} × (1 + {{increasePercent}}%) = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Your ${{currentRent}}/month rent increases {{increasePercent}}%. How much extra will you pay per month?
explanationTemplate: Monthly increase = ${{currentRent}} × {{increasePercent}}% = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: Your lease renewal letter says rent goes up {{increasePercent}}%.
promptTemplate: Current rent: ${{currentRent}}. What will you pay per month after the increase?
explanationTemplate: New rent = ${{currentRent}} × (1 + {{increasePercent}}%) = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Rent was ${{currentRent}}. After a {{increasePercent}}% hike, what's the new monthly rent?
explanationTemplate: New rent = ${{currentRent}} + ({{increasePercent}}% of ${{currentRent}}) = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Rent is ${{monthlyRent}}/month. Move-in requires first month, last month, and a security deposit (one month's rent each). Total due at signing?
explanationTemplate: 3 × ${{monthlyRent}} = ${{answer}}. First + last + deposit — that's 3 months' rent upfront.

scenarioTemplate: You found an apartment listed at ${{monthlyRent}}/month.
promptTemplate: The landlord wants first, last, and one month's security deposit. How much do you need upfront?
explanationTemplate: 3 × ${{monthlyRent}} = ${{answer}}. Always budget for 3 months' rent at move-in.

promptTemplate: Rent: ${{monthlyRent}}/month. Move-in costs: first + last + security deposit (all one month each) plus a ${{brokerFee}} broker fee. Total?
explanationTemplate: (3 × ${{monthlyRent}}) + ${{brokerFee}} broker = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: You found an apartment for ${{monthlyRent}}/month in a city that requires a broker fee.
promptTemplate: First, last, and security deposit (each equal to one month's rent) plus a ${{brokerFee}} broker fee. How much cash do you need?
explanationTemplate: 3 months' rent (${{monthlyRent}} × 3) + ${{brokerFee}} broker = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: You're signing a lease on a ${{monthlyRent}}/month apartment.
promptTemplate: The landlord requires first month, last month, and a security deposit equal to one month's rent. Total move-in cost?
explanationTemplate: 3 × ${{monthlyRent}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: An apartment rents for ${{monthlyRent}}/month and is {{squareFeet}} sq ft. What's the price per square foot?
explanationTemplate: ${{monthlyRent}} ÷ {{squareFeet}} sqft = ${{answer}}/sqft.

promptTemplate: A {{squareFeet}} sq ft apartment costs ${{monthlyRent}}/month. Price per square foot?
explanationTemplate: Price/sqft = ${{monthlyRent}} ÷ {{squareFeet}} = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: You're comparing two apartments. This one is {{squareFeet}} sq ft for ${{monthlyRent}}/month.
promptTemplate: What's the cost per square foot?
explanationTemplate: ${{monthlyRent}} ÷ {{squareFeet}} = ${{answer}}/sqft. Lower means better value.

promptTemplate: Rent: ${{monthlyRent}}/month. Size: {{squareFeet}} sq ft. What do you pay per square foot?
explanationTemplate: ${{monthlyRent}} ÷ {{squareFeet}} sqft = ${{answer}}/sqft.

promptTemplate: A {{squareFeet}} sq ft studio for ${{monthlyRent}}/month. How much per square foot?
explanationTemplate: ${{monthlyRent}} ÷ {{squareFeet}} = ${{answer}}/sqft.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanAmount}} at {{annualRate}}% over {{loanYears}} years. Estimate the monthly payment (interest + principal).
explanationTemplate: Monthly ≈ interest (${{loanAmount}} × {{annualRate}}% ÷ 12) + principal (${{loanAmount}} ÷ {{loanYears}} × 12) = ~${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: A ${{loanAmount}} mortgage at {{annualRate}}% for {{loanYears}} years. Rough monthly payment?
explanationTemplate: Interest portion + principal portion ≈ ${{answer}}/month.

scenarioTemplate: You're buying a home with a ${{loanAmount}} loan at {{annualRate}}% for {{loanYears}} years.
promptTemplate: Estimate your monthly payment.
explanationTemplate: Monthly ≈ ${{answer}}. This is a rough estimate — real amortization is slightly different.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanAmount}} at {{annualRate}}% for {{loanYears}} years. Approximate monthly cost?
explanationTemplate: ${{answer}}/month estimated from interest + principal share.

promptTemplate: A ${{loanAmount}} mortgage at {{annualRate}}% over {{loanYears}} years. What's the rough monthly payment?
explanationTemplate: ~${{answer}}/month. Compare this to local rents to decide.
scenarioTemplate: You're deciding whether to buy or keep renting.

promptTemplate: Income: ${{taxableIncome}}. First ${{bracket1Limit}} taxed at {{rate1}}%, the rest at {{rate2}}%. Total tax?
explanationTemplate: First ${{bracket1Limit}} at {{rate1}}% + remainder at {{rate2}}% = ${{answer}}. Marginal — not flat.

promptTemplate: Taxable income: ${{taxableIncome}}. Tax brackets: {{rate1}}% up to ${{bracket1Limit}}, then {{rate2}}%. How much tax?
explanationTemplate: ${{bracket1Limit}} × {{rate1}}% + (${{taxableIncome}} − ${{bracket1Limit}}) × {{rate2}}% = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: You earned ${{taxableIncome}} this year.
promptTemplate: Tax brackets: {{rate1}}% on the first ${{bracket1Limit}}, {{rate2}}% above. Calculate your total tax.
explanationTemplate: (${{bracket1Limit}} × {{rate1}}%) + (${{taxableIncome}} − ${{bracket1Limit}}) × {{rate2}}% = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Income: ${{taxableIncome}}. Brackets: {{rate1}}% up to ${{bracket1Limit}}, {{rate2}}% beyond. Tax owed?
explanationTemplate: Marginal tax = ${{answer}}. Only income above the bracket limit is taxed at the higher rate.

promptTemplate: Taxable income: ${{taxableIncome}}. First ${{bracket1Limit}} is taxed at {{rate1}}%, the rest at {{rate2}}%. What's the total tax?
explanationTemplate: Tax = (${{bracket1Limit}} × {{rate1}}%) + (${{taxableIncome}} − ${{bracket1Limit}}) × {{rate2}}% = ${{answer}}.
scenarioTemplate: You're estimating how much you'll owe at tax time.

promptTemplate: Gross pay: ${{grossPay}}. FICA: {{ficaRate}}%, federal: {{federalRate}}%, state: {{stateRate}}%. What's your net pay?
explanationTemplate: Total deductions = {{ficaRate}}% + {{federalRate}}% + {{stateRate}}%. Net = ${{grossPay}} × remaining = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Your biweekly gross is ${{grossPay}}. After {{ficaRate}}% FICA, {{federalRate}}% federal, and {{stateRate}}% state tax, what's your take-home?
explanationTemplate: Net = ${{grossPay}} × (1 − total deductions) = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Gross pay: ${{grossPay}}. Deductions: FICA {{ficaRate}}%, federal {{federalRate}}%, state {{stateRate}}%. Net pay?
explanationTemplate: Total rate = {{ficaRate}} + {{federalRate}} + {{stateRate}} = deduction total. Net = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: Your paycheck stub shows ${{grossPay}} gross.
promptTemplate: After {{ficaRate}}% FICA, {{federalRate}}% federal, {{stateRate}}% state — what hits your bank account?
explanationTemplate: ${{grossPay}} × (1 − total rate) = ${{answer}} deposited.

promptTemplate: Gross pay: ${{grossPay}}. Deductions: FICA {{ficaRate}}%, federal {{federalRate}}%, state {{stateRate}}%. What do you actually take home?
explanationTemplate: Net = ${{grossPay}} after removing {{ficaRate}}% + {{federalRate}}% + {{stateRate}}% = ${{answer}}.
scenarioTemplate: You're comparing two job offers and want to know the real take-home.

promptTemplate: Annual salary: ${{annualSalary}}. Total deductions: {{totalDeductionRate}}%. What's your monthly take-home?
explanationTemplate: ${{annualSalary}} × (1 − {{totalDeductionRate}}%) ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{annualSalary}}/year with {{totalDeductionRate}}% total deductions. Monthly take-home?
explanationTemplate: Net annual = ${{annualSalary}} × (1 − {{totalDeductionRate}}%), then ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}/month.

scenarioTemplate: A job offer says ${{annualSalary}}/year.
promptTemplate: With {{totalDeductionRate}}% total deductions, what will you actually take home monthly?
explanationTemplate: ${{annualSalary}} × (1 − {{totalDeductionRate}}%) ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}. This is your real budget number.

promptTemplate: Salary: ${{annualSalary}}/year. Deductions: {{totalDeductionRate}}%. Monthly take-home?
explanationTemplate: Monthly net = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: ${{annualSalary}} annual salary, {{totalDeductionRate}}% deducted. What's your monthly deposit?
explanationTemplate: ${{annualSalary}} × (1 − {{totalDeductionRate}}%) ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You had ${{totalWithheld}} withheld this year and owe ${{taxOwed}} in taxes. What's your refund?
explanationTemplate: Refund = ${{totalWithheld}} − ${{taxOwed}} = ${{answer}}. Positive means money back.

promptTemplate: Total withheld: ${{totalWithheld}}. Tax owed: ${{taxOwed}}. How much is your refund?
explanationTemplate: ${{totalWithheld}} − ${{taxOwed}} = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: Tax time! Your W-2 shows ${{totalWithheld}} withheld.
promptTemplate: Your tax software says you owe ${{taxOwed}}. How much is your refund?
explanationTemplate: Refund = withheld − owed = ${{totalWithheld}} − ${{taxOwed}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You had ${{totalWithheld}} withheld. You owe ${{taxOwed}}. Refund amount?
explanationTemplate: ${{totalWithheld}} − ${{taxOwed}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Your employer withheld ${{totalWithheld}} over the year. You owe ${{taxOwed}}. What's your refund?
explanationTemplate: Refund = ${{totalWithheld}} − ${{taxOwed}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You earned ${{freelanceIncome}} freelancing. Self-employment tax is 15.3%. How much SE tax do you owe?
explanationTemplate: SE tax = ${{freelanceIncome}} × 15.3% = ${{answer}}. This covers both sides of FICA.

promptTemplate: Gig income: ${{freelanceIncome}}. Calculate the 15.3% self-employment tax.
explanationTemplate: ${{freelanceIncome}} × 0.153 = ${{answer}}.

scenarioTemplate: You did freelance design work and earned ${{freelanceIncome}}.
promptTemplate: How much self-employment tax (15.3%) will you owe?
explanationTemplate: SE tax = ${{freelanceIncome}} × 15.3% = ${{answer}}. Plan to set aside 30%+ total.

promptTemplate: Freelance earnings: ${{freelanceIncome}}. Self-employment tax at 15.3%. Amount owed?
explanationTemplate: ${{freelanceIncome}} × 0.153 = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You made ${{freelanceIncome}} this quarter from freelancing. What's the 15.3% SE tax?
explanationTemplate: SE tax = ${{freelanceIncome}} × 15.3% = ${{answer}}. File quarterly to avoid penalties.

promptTemplate: Your employer matches {{matchPercent}}% of your ${{contribution}} annual 401(k) contribution. How much free money do you get?
explanationTemplate: Match = contribution × match%. ${{contribution}} × {{matchPercent}}% = your employer's free contribution.

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{contribution}} to your 401(k). Your employer matches {{matchPercent}}%. What's the total going into your account?
explanationTemplate: Total = your contribution + employer match. ${{contribution}} + ({{matchPercent}}% of ${{contribution}}). Always contribute enough to max the match.

scenarioTemplate: Your company offers a 401(k) match and you want to know how much extra you're getting.
promptTemplate: You earn ${{annualSalary}} and contribute {{contribPercent}}% to your 401(k). Your employer matches {{matchPercent}}% of your contribution. What's the employer match amount?
explanationTemplate: Your contribution = ${{annualSalary}} × {{contribPercent}}%. Employer match = that × {{matchPercent}}%. Not maxing the match = leaving free money on the table.

promptTemplate: Your employer matches 50% of your contribution up to 6% of your ${{annualSalary}} salary. You contribute 6%. What's the employer's annual match?
explanationTemplate: 6% of ${{annualSalary}} is your contribution. 50% of that is the match. This is the most common match structure in the US.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{annualSalary}} and contribute {{contribPercent}}% to your 401(k). Your employer matches {{matchPercent}}%. What's the total annual amount going into your 401(k)?
explanationTemplate: Your contribution + employer match. ${{annualSalary}} × {{contribPercent}}% × (1 + {{matchPercent}}%). Both pieces grow tax-deferred.

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{contribution}} to a Roth IRA. Your tax rate is {{taxRate}}%. How much tax do you pay on this contribution?
explanationTemplate: Roth contributions are after-tax: ${{contribution}} × {{taxRate}}% = tax you pay now. The upside? Zero tax on withdrawals in retirement.

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{contribution}} to a Traditional IRA. Your tax rate is {{taxRate}}%. How much do you save on taxes this year?
explanationTemplate: Traditional contributions reduce taxable income: ${{contribution}} × {{taxRate}}% = your tax break now. You'll pay tax when you withdraw in retirement.

scenarioTemplate: You're deciding between Roth and Traditional IRA contributions.
promptTemplate: You contribute ${{contribution}} to a Roth IRA at a {{taxRate}}% tax rate. What's the after-tax cost of this contribution (contribution + tax)?
explanationTemplate: With Roth, you pay tax upfront: ${{contribution}} goes into the IRA, plus ${{contribution}} × {{taxRate}}% in tax. Total out of pocket = contribution + tax.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{annualSalary}} and contribute ${{contribution}} to a Traditional IRA. At a {{taxRate}}% tax rate, what's your net cost after the tax deduction?
explanationTemplate: Net cost = contribution − tax saved. You contribute ${{contribution}} but save ${{contribution}} × {{taxRate}}% in taxes. Traditional costs less today but is taxed later.

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{contribution}} at {{taxRate}}% tax rate. How much more does a Roth cost you today compared to a Traditional IRA?
explanationTemplate: The Roth costs ${{contribution}} × {{taxRate}}% more today (you pay tax now). Traditional saves that amount now but you'll pay it in retirement.

promptTemplate: You invest ${{monthlyAmount}} per month for {{years}} years. How much have you contributed in total (ignoring growth)?
explanationTemplate: Total contributed = ${{monthlyAmount}} × 12 × {{years}}. This is your baseline — compound growth adds more on top.

promptTemplate: You invested ${{totalContributed}} over time and your account is now worth ${{finalValue}}. How much came from investment growth?
explanationTemplate: Growth = final value − contributions. ${{finalValue}} − ${{totalContributed}} = money your money earned for you.

scenarioTemplate: You're planning for the next decade of investing.
promptTemplate: You invest ${{monthlyAmount}} per month. After 10 years, you'll have contributed ${{totalContributed}}. If the account grew to ${{finalValue}}, what's the growth amount?
explanationTemplate: Growth = ${{finalValue}} − ${{totalContributed}}. In 10 years at ~8%, you earn about 50% on top of contributions.

promptTemplate: You invest ${{monthlyAmount}}/month for 20 years (total contributed: ${{totalContributed}}). Account value: ${{finalValue}}. How much is growth?
explanationTemplate: ${{finalValue}} − ${{totalContributed}} = growth. After 20 years, compound interest often exceeds your total contributions.

promptTemplate: You invest ${{monthlyAmount}} per month for {{years}} years. Total contributions: ${{totalContributed}}. The account grew by ${{growthAmount}}. What's the final account value?
explanationTemplate: Final value = contributions + growth. ${{totalContributed}} + ${{growthAmount}}. Time is the biggest factor in compound growth.

promptTemplate: You get a {{raisePercent}}% raise but inflation is {{inflationPercent}}%. What's your real raise percentage?
explanationTemplate: Real raise = {{raisePercent}}% − {{inflationPercent}}% inflation. If inflation exceeds your raise, you're actually losing purchasing power.

promptTemplate: Your ${{annualSalary}} salary gets a {{raisePercent}}% raise. But inflation is {{inflationPercent}}%. What's the real dollar change in your purchasing power?
explanationTemplate: Real change = salary × (raise% − inflation%). ${{annualSalary}} × ({{raisePercent}}% − {{inflationPercent}}%). Positive = real gain. Negative = pay cut.

scenarioTemplate: You're evaluating whether your annual raise keeps up with the cost of living.
promptTemplate: Your salary is ${{annualSalary}}. You got a {{raisePercent}}% raise. Inflation this year was {{inflationPercent}}%. How much more (or less) can you actually buy per year?
explanationTemplate: Raise gives ${{annualSalary}} × {{raisePercent}}%. But inflation costs you ${{annualSalary}} × {{inflationPercent}}%. The difference is your real change.

promptTemplate: Offer A: {{raisePercentA}}% raise. Offer B: {{raisePercentB}}% raise. Inflation is {{inflationPercent}}%. What's the real raise for Offer A?
explanationTemplate: Real raise = nominal raise − inflation. {{raisePercentA}}% − {{inflationPercent}}% = your actual purchasing power gain.

promptTemplate: Your ${{annualSalary}} salary gets a {{raisePercent}}% raise while inflation runs at {{inflationPercent}}%. What's your new salary's purchasing power in last year's dollars?
explanationTemplate: New salary = ${{annualSalary}} × (1 + {{raisePercent}}%). In real terms, that's worth salary × (1 + raise%) / (1 + inflation%). When inflation beats your raise, you can buy less than before.

promptTemplate: Your health plan costs ${{monthlyPremium}} per month. How much do you pay in premiums per year?
explanationTemplate: Annual premium = ${{monthlyPremium}} × 12 months. This is the guaranteed cost you pay regardless of whether you visit the doctor.

promptTemplate: Your plan: ${{monthlyPremium}}/month premium, ${{deductible}} deductible. What's your maximum annual cost before coinsurance kicks in?
explanationTemplate: Worst case = annual premiums + full deductible. (${{monthlyPremium}} × 12) + ${{deductible}}. This is the most you'd pay before the plan starts sharing costs.

promptTemplate: Plan A costs ${{premiumA}}/month. Plan B costs ${{premiumB}}/month. How much more does Plan A cost per year in premiums?
explanationTemplate: Difference = (${{premiumA}} − ${{premiumB}}) × 12. Higher premiums usually mean lower deductibles — the tradeoff is guaranteed cost vs. risk.

promptTemplate: Plan: ${{monthlyPremium}}/month premium, ${{deductible}} deductible. You expect ${{medicalBills}} in medical bills this year. What's your total cost (premiums + what you pay toward bills)?
explanationTemplate: If bills < deductible, you pay premiums + full bills. Total = (${{monthlyPremium}} × 12) + ${{medicalBills}}. The deductible means insurance doesn't kick in until you've spent that amount.

promptTemplate: Plan A: ${{premiumA}}/month, ${{deductibleA}} deductible. Plan B: ${{premiumB}}/month, ${{deductibleB}} deductible. If you hit your full deductible, which plan costs less total and by how much?
explanationTemplate: Plan A total = (${{premiumA}} × 12) + ${{deductibleA}}. Plan B total = (${{premiumB}} × 12) + ${{deductibleB}}. The cheaper plan depends on how much medical care you actually use.

promptTemplate: After meeting your deductible, your coinsurance is {{coinsurancePercent}}%. You have a ${{billAmount}} procedure. How much is your share?
explanationTemplate: Your share = ${{billAmount}} × {{coinsurancePercent}}%. Coinsurance means you split costs with your insurer after the deductible is met.

promptTemplate: Your copay is ${{copayAmount}} per visit. If you visit the doctor {{visitCount}} times this year, what's your total copay spending?
explanationTemplate: Total copays = ${{copayAmount}} × {{visitCount}} visits. Copays are flat fees per visit — they don't count toward your deductible on most plans.

promptTemplate: You have a ${{totalBill}} hospital bill. Your ${{deductible}} deductible is already met. Your coinsurance is {{coinsurancePercent}}%. What do you owe?
explanationTemplate: Deductible already met, so you just pay coinsurance: ${{totalBill}} × {{coinsurancePercent}}%. The insurer covers the other {{coinsurancePercent}}% complement.

promptTemplate: You pay ${{copayPrimary}} per primary care visit and ${{copaySpecialist}} per specialist visit. You see your doctor {{primaryVisits}} times and a specialist {{specialistVisits}} times. Total copays?
explanationTemplate: Total = (primary copay × visits) + (specialist copay × visits). (${{copayPrimary}} × {{primaryVisits}}) + (${{copaySpecialist}} × {{specialistVisits}}). Specialist copays are almost always higher.

promptTemplate: You have a ${{totalBill}} bill. Deductible is ${{deductible}} (not yet met). After deductible, coinsurance is {{coinsurancePercent}}%. What's your total out-of-pocket for this bill?
explanationTemplate: You pay the full deductible (${{deductible}}) first. Then coinsurance on the rest: (${{totalBill}} − ${{deductible}}) × {{coinsurancePercent}}%. Add both parts together.

promptTemplate: You've paid ${{amountPaid}} in deductibles and coinsurance so far. Your out-of-pocket max is ${{oopMax}}. How much more could you owe this year?
explanationTemplate: Remaining = OOP max − amount paid = ${{oopMax}} − ${{amountPaid}}. After hitting your OOP max, insurance covers 100% of covered services.

promptTemplate: Your out-of-pocket max is ${{oopMax}}. You've already paid ${{amountPaid}}. A new procedure would cost you ${{procedureCost}} in coinsurance. How much will you actually pay?
explanationTemplate: You can only owe up to ${{oopMax}} − ${{amountPaid}} more. If the procedure's coinsurance exceeds that, you pay only the remaining amount to hit your max.

promptTemplate: Deductible: ${{deductible}}. Coinsurance: {{coinsurancePercent}}%. OOP max: ${{oopMax}}. You have ${{totalBill}} in medical bills. What do you pay total?
explanationTemplate: Deductible (${{deductible}}) + coinsurance on the rest. But never more than the OOP max (${{oopMax}}). The OOP max is your safety net for big medical years.

promptTemplate: Plan A: ${{oopMaxA}} OOP max. Plan B: ${{oopMaxB}} OOP max. In a worst-case year, how much more would Plan B cost you?
explanationTemplate: Difference = ${{oopMaxB}} − ${{oopMaxA}}. In a catastrophic year, the OOP max is what matters most — it's your true worst-case exposure.

promptTemplate: Plan: ${{monthlyPremium}}/month, ${{deductible}} deductible, {{coinsurancePercent}}% coinsurance, ${{oopMax}} OOP max. What's your absolute maximum annual cost including premiums?
explanationTemplate: Max cost = annual premiums + OOP max. (${{monthlyPremium}} × 12) + ${{oopMax}}. Premiums are separate from OOP max — this is the true worst case.

promptTemplate: An HDHP charges ${{hdhpPremium}}/month. A PPO charges ${{ppoPremium}}/month. How much more per year does the PPO cost in premiums?
explanationTemplate: PPO extra = (${{ppoPremium}} − ${{hdhpPremium}}) × 12. HDHPs save on premiums but have higher deductibles — the tradeoff depends on how much care you use.

promptTemplate: Your PPO costs ${{monthlyPremium}} per month with a ${{copayAmount}} copay per visit. If you go {{visitCount}} times, what's your total annual cost?
explanationTemplate: PPO total = (premium × 12) + (copay × visits). (${{monthlyPremium}} × 12) + (${{copayAmount}} × {{visitCount}}). PPOs cost more monthly but less per visit.

promptTemplate: HDHP: ${{hdhpPremium}}/month, ${{hdhpDeductible}} deductible. PPO: ${{ppoPremium}}/month. How much more does the PPO cost in premiums per year?
explanationTemplate: PPO premium extra = (${{ppoPremium}} − ${{hdhpPremium}}) × 12. This premium savings is why many healthy people choose HDHPs — plus HSA access.

promptTemplate: HDHP: ${{hdhpPremium}}/month + ${{hdhpDeductible}} deductible. PPO: ${{ppoPremium}}/month + ${{ppoCopay}} × {{visits}} visits. Which costs less if you hit the HDHP deductible?
explanationTemplate: HDHP total = (${{hdhpPremium}} × 12) + ${{hdhpDeductible}}. PPO total = (${{ppoPremium}} × 12) + (${{ppoCopay}} × {{visits}}). Compare both to find the savings.

promptTemplate: HDHP: ${{hdhpPremium}}/month, ${{hdhpDeductible}} deductible. PPO: ${{ppoPremium}}/month, ${{ppoCopay}} copay. You'll definitely hit the HDHP deductible. What's the cost difference between the plans?
explanationTemplate: HDHP total = (${{hdhpPremium}} × 12) + ${{hdhpDeductible}}. PPO total = ${{ppoPremium}} × 12 (copay is small). The gap shows how much your health usage changes the math.

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{hsaContribution}} to your HSA. Your tax rate is {{taxRate}}%. How much do you save in taxes?
explanationTemplate: Tax saving = ${{hsaContribution}} × {{taxRate}}%. HSA contributions are pre-tax — every dollar you put in saves you {{taxRate}} cents in taxes.

promptTemplate: A ${{expenseCost}} doctor visit paid with HSA funds. Your tax bracket is {{taxRate}}%. What's the real after-tax cost to you?
explanationTemplate: Effective cost = ${{expenseCost}} − (${{expenseCost}} × {{taxRate}}%). HSA money is pre-tax, so you save your tax rate on every dollar spent.

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{hsaContribution}} to your HSA at a {{taxRate}}% tax rate. A medical expense costs ${{expenseCost}}. If you pay from your HSA, what's the effective cost after tax savings?
explanationTemplate: Effective cost = expense − tax savings on that amount. ${{expenseCost}} − (${{expenseCost}} × {{taxRate}}%). Paying from HSA makes every medical dollar cheaper.

promptTemplate: HDHP: ${{hdhpPremium}}/month + you save ${{hsaTaxSaving}} in HSA taxes. PPO: ${{ppoPremium}}/month. What's the HDHP's net premium advantage per year?
explanationTemplate: Net advantage = premium savings + HSA tax savings. ((${{ppoPremium}} − ${{hdhpPremium}}) × 12) + ${{hsaTaxSaving}}. The HSA tax benefit is like getting a discount on your healthcare.

promptTemplate: You max out your HSA at ${{hsaContribution}} per year. Tax rate: {{taxRate}}%. If you invest it and don't touch it for {{years}} years, you save ${{hsaContribution}} × {{taxRate}}% in taxes each year. Total tax savings over {{years}} years?
explanationTemplate: Total tax savings = (${{hsaContribution}} × {{taxRate}}%) × {{years}} years. Over time, the HSA tax advantage compounds into serious money.

promptTemplate: Your car payment is ${{monthlyPayment}} per month for {{loanTermMonths}} months. What's the total you'll pay?
explanationTemplate: Total = ${{monthlyPayment}} × {{loanTermMonths}} months. That low monthly payment adds up — always check the total cost, not just the monthly number.

promptTemplate: You borrow ${{loanAmount}} for a car. Your total payments will be ${{totalPaid}}. How much interest do you pay?
explanationTemplate: Interest = total paid − loan amount = ${{totalPaid}} − ${{loanAmount}}. This is the real cost of borrowing — the price tag is only part of the story.

promptTemplate: You're looking at a ${{carPrice}} car with a ${{downPayment}} down payment. If the remaining ${{loanAmount}} is financed at ${{monthlyPayment}}/month for {{termMonths}} months, how much total do you spend including the down payment?
explanationTemplate: Total cost = down payment + (monthly × months). ${{downPayment}} + (${{monthlyPayment}} × {{termMonths}}). Compare this to the sticker price to see how much interest costs you.

promptTemplate: Option A: ${{paymentA}}/month for {{termA}} months. Option B: ${{paymentB}}/month for {{termB}} months. How much more does the longer loan cost in total?
explanationTemplate: Option A total = ${{paymentA}} × {{termA}}. Option B total = ${{paymentB}} × {{termB}}. Lower monthly payments often mean higher total cost — that's the trap of longer loans.

promptTemplate: You borrow ${{loanAmount}} for a car. At ${{payment60}}/month for 60 months, total is ${{total60}}. At ${{payment72}}/month for 72 months, total is ${{total72}}. How much extra interest does the longer term cost?
explanationTemplate: Extra interest = longer loan interest − shorter loan interest. (${{total72}} − ${{loanAmount}}) − (${{total60}} − ${{loanAmount}}). The monthly savings comes with a hidden interest cost.

promptTemplate: A ${{monthlyPayment}}/month car payment for {{termYears}} years. What's the total you'll pay?
explanationTemplate: Total = ${{monthlyPayment}} × {{termYears}} years × 12 months. Convert years to months first, then multiply by payment.

promptTemplate: 5-year loan: ${{payment5}} per month. 6-year loan: ${{payment6}} per month. How much less per month is the longer loan?
explanationTemplate: Monthly savings = ${{payment5}} − ${{payment6}}. Looks good monthly, but check the total cost — that lower payment adds 12 more months of interest.

promptTemplate: You can afford ${{budget}} per month for a car. At {{termYears}} years, how much total can you spend on a car loan?
explanationTemplate: Total = ${{budget}} × {{termYears}} × 12. This is the maximum loan amount plus interest you can handle — not the car price you can afford.

promptTemplate: You borrow ${{loanAmount}}. A 48-month loan: ${{payment48}}/month. A 72-month loan: ${{payment72}}/month. How much more total interest does the 72-month loan cost?
explanationTemplate: 48-mo interest = (${{payment48}} × 48) − ${{loanAmount}}. 72-mo interest = (${{payment72}} × 72) − ${{loanAmount}}. The difference is pure extra cost from stretching the loan.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanAmount}}. Option A: ${{paymentA}}/month × {{termA}} months. Option B: ${{paymentB}}/month × {{termB}} months. What percentage of each loan total is interest? Give Option B's interest percentage.
explanationTemplate: Interest = (payment × months) − loan. Interest % = interest / total × 100. Longer loans mean a bigger chunk of every payment goes to the bank, not your car.

promptTemplate: You want to put {{downPercent}}% down on a ${{carPrice}} car. How much is your down payment?
explanationTemplate: Down payment = ${{carPrice}} × {{downPercent}}%. A bigger down payment means a smaller loan and less interest over time.

promptTemplate: The car costs ${{carPrice}}. You put ${{downPayment}} down. How much do you need to finance?
explanationTemplate: Loan amount = ${{carPrice}} − ${{downPayment}}. Every dollar you put down is a dollar you don't pay interest on.

promptTemplate: Car price: ${{carPrice}}. You put {{downPercent}}% down. The remaining loan will cost ${{interestRate}}% in total interest. What's the total interest you'll pay?
explanationTemplate: Loan = ${{carPrice}} × (100% − {{downPercent}}%). Interest = loan × {{interestRate}}%. Bigger down payment → smaller loan → less interest.

promptTemplate: A ${{carPrice}} car. With 10% down you'd pay ${{interest10}} in interest. With 20% down you'd pay ${{interest20}} in interest. How much does the extra 10% down save you?
explanationTemplate: Savings = ${{interest10}} − ${{interest20}}. That extra down payment doesn't just reduce your loan — it reduces the interest on the loan too.

promptTemplate: Car: ${{carPrice}}. Option A: ${{downA}} down, finance rest at ${{paymentA}}/month × {{termA}} months. Option B: ${{downB}} down, finance rest at ${{paymentB}}/month × {{termB}} months. Total cost difference?
explanationTemplate: Total A = ${{downA}} + (${{paymentA}} × {{termA}}). Total B = ${{downB}} + (${{paymentB}} × {{termB}}). Even though B requires more cash upfront, it can save thousands overall.

promptTemplate: The 10% rule: car payments shouldn't exceed 10% of your monthly income. You earn ${{monthlyIncome}}/month. What's your max car payment?
explanationTemplate: Max payment = ${{monthlyIncome}} × 10%. This keeps transportation costs from eating into other financial goals.

promptTemplate: The 20/4/10 rule says put 20% down. On a ${{carPrice}} car, how much is that?
explanationTemplate: 20% down = ${{carPrice}} × 20%. The 20/4/10 rule: 20% down, 4-year loan max, 10% of income max payment.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{annualSalary}} per year. Using the 10% rule, what's the maximum you should pay monthly for a car?
explanationTemplate: Monthly income = ${{annualSalary}} ÷ 12. Max payment = monthly income × 10%. Two steps: divide by 12, then take 10%.

promptTemplate: Income: ${{monthlyIncome}}/month. A car you like is ${{carPrice}} with ${{monthlyPayment}}/month payments. Does this pass the 10% rule? By how much are you over or under?
explanationTemplate: Budget = ${{monthlyIncome}} × 10%. Difference = budget − ${{monthlyPayment}}. If negative, the car is too expensive for your income by the 10% rule.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{monthlyIncome}}/month. Following 20/4/10: 20% down, 4-year max, 10% payment max. Your max payment is 10% of income for 48 months, plus your 20% down. What's the most expensive car you can buy?
explanationTemplate: Max payment = ${{monthlyIncome}} × 10%. Max financed = payment × 48. That's 80% of car price (you put 20% down). So max car = financed ÷ 0.80.

promptTemplate: You buy a ${{carPrice}} car. It loses {{depPercent}}% of its value in the first year. What's it worth after year 1?
explanationTemplate: Value after year 1 = ${{carPrice}} × (100% − {{depPercent}}%). New cars lose the most value in year one — that's the depreciation hit.

promptTemplate: A ${{carPrice}} car depreciates {{depPercent}}% in its first year. How much value does it lose?
explanationTemplate: Depreciation = ${{carPrice}} × {{depPercent}}%. This is money you'll never get back — it's the hidden cost of buying new.

promptTemplate: A ${{carPrice}} car loses {{depYear1}}% in year 1 and another {{depYear2}}% of remaining value in year 2. What's it worth after 2 years?
explanationTemplate: Year 1 value = ${{carPrice}} × (1 − {{depYear1}}%). Year 2 value = Year 1 value × (1 − {{depYear2}}%). Each year's depreciation is on the lower remaining value.

promptTemplate: You buy a ${{carPrice}} car. After 3 years it's worth ${{valueAfter3}}. How much total value has it lost?
explanationTemplate: Total depreciation = purchase price − current value = ${{carPrice}} − ${{valueAfter3}}. A car that's 2-3 years old has already taken the biggest depreciation hit.

promptTemplate: New car: ${{newPrice}}, worth ${{newValueY3}} after 3 years. Used car (2 years old): ${{usedPrice}}, worth ${{usedValueY3}} after 3 more years. Which loses less in depreciation and by how much?
explanationTemplate: New loss = ${{newPrice}} − ${{newValueY3}}. Used loss = ${{usedPrice}} − ${{usedValueY3}}. Buying used lets someone else absorb the steepest depreciation.

promptTemplate: Your student loan payment is ${{monthlyPayment}} per month. How much do you pay per year?
explanationTemplate: Annual = ${{monthlyPayment}} × 12. Knowing your annual student loan cost helps you see how it fits into your overall budget.

promptTemplate: You owe ${{loanBalance}} in student loans at roughly ${{paymentPer10k}} per month for every $10,000 borrowed. What's your estimated monthly payment?
explanationTemplate: Payment = (${{loanBalance}} ÷ 10,000) × ${{paymentPer10k}}. The ~$100-$120 per $10K rule is a quick way to estimate standard 10-year repayment.

promptTemplate: You owe ${{loanBalance}} at {{interestRate}}% interest on a 10-year plan. Monthly interest alone is ${{loanBalance}} × {{interestRate}}% ÷ 12. What's the monthly interest charge?
explanationTemplate: Monthly interest = ${{loanBalance}} × {{interestRate}}% ÷ 12. Early in repayment, most of your payment goes to interest — that's why extra payments help so much.

promptTemplate: 10-year plan: ${{payment10}} per month. 20-year plan: ${{payment20}} per month. How much less per month is the extended plan?
explanationTemplate: Savings = ${{payment10}} − ${{payment20}} per month. But the 20-year plan means 10 more years of interest — always check the total cost too.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanBalance}} at {{interestRate}}%. Your payment is ${{monthlyPayment}}. Monthly interest is ${{monthlyInterest}}. How much of your first payment goes to principal?
explanationTemplate: Principal = payment − interest = ${{monthlyPayment}} − ${{monthlyInterest}}. Early on, you're mostly paying interest. As principal shrinks, more goes to actually paying off the loan.

promptTemplate: Your student loan payment is ${{monthlyPayment}}/month for {{termYears}} years. What's the total you'll pay?
explanationTemplate: Total = ${{monthlyPayment}} × {{termYears}} × 12 months. Seeing the total number is often the wake-up call that motivates faster repayment.

promptTemplate: You borrowed ${{loanAmount}}. Over {{termYears}} years you'll pay a total of ${{totalPaid}}. How much is pure interest?
explanationTemplate: Interest = total paid − borrowed = ${{totalPaid}} − ${{loanAmount}}. This is the real cost of the loan — what you pay just for the privilege of borrowing.

promptTemplate: 10-year plan: ${{payment10}}/month. 20-year plan: ${{payment20}}/month. How much more total do you pay on the 20-year plan?
explanationTemplate: 10-year total = ${{payment10}} × 120. 20-year total = ${{payment20}} × 240. The lower monthly payment costs massively more over the full life of the loan.

promptTemplate: You owe ${{loanAmount}}. Standard plan total: ${{totalStandard}}. Extended plan total: ${{totalExtended}}. What percentage more does the extended plan cost?
explanationTemplate: Extra = (${{totalExtended}} − ${{totalStandard}}) ÷ ${{totalStandard}} × 100%. The extended plan can cost 25-50% more in total even though the monthly payment feels lighter.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanAmount}} at {{interestRate}}%. You pay ${{extraMonthly}} extra per month above the minimum ${{minPayment}}. Total monthly = ${{totalPayment}}. How much do you save in total interest by paying extra? Original total: ${{originalTotal}}. New total: ${{newTotal}}.
explanationTemplate: Savings = ${{originalTotal}} − ${{newTotal}}. Every extra dollar goes straight to principal, which reduces future interest. Even $100/month extra can save thousands.

promptTemplate: Current payment: ${{oldPayment}}/month. After refinancing: ${{newPayment}}/month. How much do you save per month?
explanationTemplate: Monthly savings = ${{oldPayment}} − ${{newPayment}}. Refinancing can lower your rate, but you may lose federal loan protections like IDR and PSLF.

promptTemplate: Refinancing saves you ${{monthlySaving}} per month. How much do you save per year?
explanationTemplate: Annual savings = ${{monthlySaving}} × 12. Make sure the savings justify giving up federal loan benefits like income-driven repayment.

promptTemplate: Current: ${{oldPayment}}/month for {{remainingMonths}} months left. Refi: ${{newPayment}}/month for {{newTermMonths}} months. Which costs less total and by how much?
explanationTemplate: Current total = ${{oldPayment}} × {{remainingMonths}}. Refi total = ${{newPayment}} × {{newTermMonths}}. Compare totals, not just monthly payments — term length matters.

promptTemplate: Current rate: {{oldRate}}% on ${{loanBalance}}. Monthly interest: ${{oldInterest}}. New rate: {{newRate}}%. What would the new monthly interest be?
explanationTemplate: New monthly interest = ${{loanBalance}} × {{newRate}}% ÷ 12. Lower rate means more of each payment goes to principal instead of interest.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanBalance}}. Current: {{oldRate}}%, ${{oldPayment}}/month, {{remainingMonths}} months left (total remaining: ${{oldTotal}}). Refi: {{newRate}}%, ${{newPayment}}/month, {{newTermMonths}} months (total: ${{newTotal}}). How much do you save?
explanationTemplate: Savings = ${{oldTotal}} − ${{newTotal}}. Refinancing at a lower rate with the same term length is usually a clear win — if you don't need federal protections.

promptTemplate: On an IDR plan, you pay {{idrPercent}}% of your discretionary income. If your discretionary income is ${{discretionaryIncome}} per year, what's your annual IDR payment?
explanationTemplate: IDR payment = ${{discretionaryIncome}} × {{idrPercent}}% per year. Discretionary income = your income minus 150% of the poverty line.

promptTemplate: Your IDR annual payment is ${{annualPayment}}. What's your monthly payment?
explanationTemplate: Monthly = ${{annualPayment}} ÷ 12. IDR payments adjust each year as your income changes — they're designed to stay affordable.

promptTemplate: You earn ${{annualIncome}} per year. The poverty guideline is ${{povertyLine}}. Your discretionary income = salary − (150% × poverty line). IDR is {{idrPercent}}% of discretionary income. What's your monthly IDR payment?
explanationTemplate: Discretionary income = ${{annualIncome}} − (150% × ${{povertyLine}}). IDR = discretionary × {{idrPercent}}% ÷ 12. This formula protects low earners from unaffordable payments.

promptTemplate: Standard plan: ${{standardPayment}}/month. IDR plan: ${{idrPayment}}/month. How much less per year is the IDR plan?
explanationTemplate: Annual savings = (${{standardPayment}} − ${{idrPayment}}) × 12. But lower payments mean longer repayment and more total interest — unless you qualify for forgiveness.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanBalance}}. Standard: ${{standardPayment}}/month × 120 months = ${{standardTotal}}. IDR: ${{idrPayment}}/month × 240 months = ${{idrTotal}}, but remaining balance forgiven after 20 years. Which costs less in total payments?
explanationTemplate: Standard total = ${{standardTotal}}. IDR total = ${{idrTotal}} (then forgiveness). Compare the actual dollars paid. Note: forgiven amounts may be taxable income.

promptTemplate: Under PSLF, you make 120 qualifying payments of ${{monthlyPayment}}. What's the total you'll pay over 10 years?
explanationTemplate: Total = ${{monthlyPayment}} × 120 payments. After 10 years of qualifying payments in public service, the remaining balance is forgiven tax-free.

promptTemplate: You owe ${{loanBalance}}. After 120 PSLF payments totaling ${{totalPaid}}, the rest is forgiven. How much is forgiven?
explanationTemplate: Forgiven = balance − total paid = ${{loanBalance}} − ${{totalPaid}}. PSLF forgiveness is tax-free — unlike IDR forgiveness which may be taxable.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanBalance}}. IDR payment: ${{idrPayment}}/month. After 120 PSLF payments, how much will you have paid and how much is forgiven?
explanationTemplate: Total paid = ${{idrPayment}} × 120 = your contribution. Forgiven = ${{loanBalance}} − total paid. PSLF works best with high balances and lower IDR payments.

promptTemplate: Without PSLF: pay ${{standardPayment}}/month × 120 months = ${{standardTotal}}. With PSLF: pay ${{idrPayment}}/month × 120 months. How much do you save with PSLF?
explanationTemplate: PSLF total = ${{idrPayment}} × 120. Savings = ${{standardTotal}} − PSLF total. PSLF is most valuable for people with high debt relative to income in qualifying jobs.

promptTemplate: Loan: ${{loanBalance}}. Option A: Refinance to ${{refiPayment}}/month × {{refiMonths}} months. Option B: PSLF with ${{pslfPayment}}/month × 120 months, rest forgiven. Difference in total paid?
explanationTemplate: Refi total = ${{refiPayment}} × {{refiMonths}}. PSLF total = ${{pslfPayment}} × 120. The difference can be tens of thousands — but PSLF requires 10 years in qualifying public service.

promptTemplate: Your bill is ${{billAmount}}. Using the $20-per-$100 rule, what's a 20% tip?
explanationTemplate: For every $100, 20% = $20. ${{billAmount}} ÷ 100 = the multiplier. Multiply by $20 to get your tip.

promptTemplate: An item costs ${{price}}. You have a {{couponPct}}% coupon. How much do you save?
explanationTemplate: Coupon saving = price × coupon%. ${{price}} × {{couponPct}}% = ${{answer}} off.

promptTemplate: You pay ${{price}} on a card that gives {{cashbackPct}}% cashback. How much cash do you get back?
explanationTemplate: Cashback = amount paid × cashback%. ${{price}} × {{cashbackPct}}% = ${{answer}} back.

promptTemplate: Item ${{price}}. Apply a {{couponPct}}% coupon, then get {{cashbackPct}}% cashback on what you pay. Total saving?
explanationTemplate: Coupon first: ${{price}} × {{couponPct}}% = coupon saving. Then cashback on remainder: (${{price}} − coupon) × {{cashbackPct}}%. Add both = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Option A: {{couponPct}}% coupon on ${{price}}. Option B: {{cashbackPct}}% cashback on ${{price}}. How much more does the better option save?
explanationTemplate: Coupon saves ${{price}} × {{couponPct}}%. Cashback saves ${{price}} × {{cashbackPct}}%. Bigger % almost always wins. Difference = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Item ${{price}}. Stack a {{couponPct}}% coupon with {{cashbackPct}}% cashback (cashback applies to the discounted price). What's your final net cost?
explanationTemplate: Sale price = ${{price}} × (1 − {{couponPct}}%). Then subtract cashback × sale price. Net = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: A ${{originalPrice}} item is {{discountPercent}}% off. With {{taxPercent}}% sales tax, what do you pay at checkout?
explanationTemplate: Discount first: ${{originalPrice}} × (1 − {{discountPercent}}%) = sale price. Then add tax: × (1 + {{taxPercent}}%). Final = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Item ${{originalPrice}}, {{discountPercent}}% off, {{taxPercent}}% tax. How much sales tax do you pay (on the discounted price)?
explanationTemplate: Sale price = ${{originalPrice}} × (1 − {{discountPercent}}%). Tax = sale price × {{taxPercent}}% = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: A ${{originalPrice}} item has {{discountPercent}}% off and {{taxPercent}}% sales tax. What's the total at checkout?
explanationTemplate: Sale price × (1 + tax). ${{originalPrice}} × (1 − {{discountPercent}}%) × (1 + {{taxPercent}}%) = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: ${{originalPrice}} item: {{firstDiscount}}% off, then {{secondDiscount}}% off, then {{taxPercent}}% tax. What's the total?
explanationTemplate: Apply discounts one at a time, then tax. ${{originalPrice}} × (1 − {{firstDiscount}}%) × (1 − {{secondDiscount}}%) × (1 + {{taxPercent}}%) = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: ${{originalPrice}} item. Compare paying full price + {{taxPercent}}% tax vs {{discountPercent}}% off + {{taxPercent}}% tax. How much do you save with the discount?
explanationTemplate: Saving = ${{originalPrice}} × {{discountPercent}}% × (1 + {{taxPercent}}%). You save both the discount AND the tax on the discount = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: DashPass costs ${{monthlyFee}}/month and saves ${{savingPerUse}} per order. How many orders per month do you need to break even?
explanationTemplate: Break-even = fee ÷ saving per use. ${{monthlyFee}} ÷ ${{savingPerUse}} = {{answer}} orders, rounded up.

promptTemplate: Costco membership is ${{annualFee}}/year. You save ${{savingPerUse}} per visit. How many visits per year to break even?
explanationTemplate: Break-even = fee ÷ saving per use. ${{annualFee}} ÷ ${{savingPerUse}} = {{answer}} visits, rounded up.

promptTemplate: Uber One: ${{monthlyFee}}/month, saves ${{savingPerUse}}/ride. You take {{usesPerPeriod}} rides this month. Net monthly saving after the fee?
explanationTemplate: (uses × saving) − fee. ({{usesPerPeriod}} × ${{savingPerUse}}) − ${{monthlyFee}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: DashPass: ${{feeA}}/mo, saves ${{saveA}}/use. Uber One: ${{feeB}}/mo, saves ${{saveB}}/use. What's the difference in break-even uses between the two?
explanationTemplate: Plan A break-even = ${{feeA}}/${{saveA}}. Plan B = ${{feeB}}/${{saveB}}. Difference = {{answer}} uses.

promptTemplate: Costco ${{annualFee}}/year, saves ${{savingPerUse}}/visit. You go {{usesPerPeriod}} times/year. What's your annual net saving?
explanationTemplate: ({{usesPerPeriod}} visits × ${{savingPerUse}}) − ${{annualFee}} fee = ${{answer}} annual net.
